nameStory: The hypoxylon canker gets its name from its ability to cause cankers - those sunken, diseased areas of bark that look like wounds on tree trunks. The 'hypoxylon' part comes from an old scientific name for this group of fungi, referring to their wood-loving nature (hypo meaning 'under' and xylon meaning 'wood' in Greek).
description: Hypoxylon canker is a parasitic fungus that attacks trees, creating dark, crusty patches on bark and eventually killing branches or entire trees. The fungus forms hard, blackish stromata (fungal structures) that look like charcoal bumps scattered across the bark surface. These structures can range from small dots to larger patches several inches across. It's not a mushroom you'd find growing from soil, but rather a tree disease that becomes visible as dark, crusty growths on infected bark.

idTips.label: Dark crusty patches
idTips.description: Look for hard, blackish or dark gray crusty areas on tree bark that feel rough and bumpy to the touch, like charcoal or burnt toast

idTips.label: Sunken cankers
idTips.description: The infected bark areas often appear sunken or depressed compared to healthy bark, creating visible wounds or indentations on the trunk

idTips.label: Tiny dark dots
idTips.description: Close examination reveals numerous tiny black dots (spore-producing structures) embedded in the crusty surface, visible with a hand lens

idTips.label: Brittle texture
idTips.description: The fungal crust is brittle and may flake off when touched, revealing diseased wood underneath that's often discolored

idTips.label: Branch dieback
idTips.description: Infected trees show dying branches above the canker, with leaves that wilt, turn brown, or drop prematurely

habitat: Found on various hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, particularly on oaks, maples, and other deciduous species. Look for it in both mature forests and woodland edges, from sea level to moderate elevations. The fungus tends to attack stressed trees, so you're more likely to find it in areas affected by drought, construction damage, or other environmental stresses.

seasonality.spring: Fresh infections may become visible as bark begins to show stress from the growing fungus. Look for new areas of discolored or slightly sunken bark.
seasonality.summer: The dark crusty stromata become most prominent during warm weather, when the fungus is actively producing spores. This is the best time to spot the characteristic blackish patches.
seasonality.fall: Infected branches show obvious dieback with prematurely dropping leaves or branches that failed to leaf out properly. The contrast makes identification easier.
seasonality.winter: The dark crusty patches remain visible against bare bark and may be easier to spot without leaves obscuring the view. Infected branches are clearly dead.

funFact: This fungus is like a tree's worst nightmare house guest - it actually waits for trees to become stressed from drought or injury before launching its attack, taking advantage of weakened defenses to move in and take over!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other dark bark fungi or even fire damage, but hypoxylon canker's crusty texture with tiny embedded dots is distinctive. Remember: if it feels like rough charcoal and has pinpoint black dots, it's likely hypoxylon canker rather than just burnt or weathered bark.
contextualKnowledge: This fungus was formerly classified in the genus Hypoxylon, so you may still see it referred to as 'Hypoxylon canker' in older field guides and forestry literature. The name change to Biscogniauxia is relatively recent, reflecting advances in fungal DNA analysis.
compareHints: Biscogniauxia atropunctata typically forms larger, more extensive crusty patches compared to its relatives like B. marginata, which tends to create more defined, smaller stromata with distinct margins. The 'atropunctata' (meaning 'black-dotted') species also has more densely packed spore-producing dots, giving it a more uniformly dark, peppered appearance than other Biscogniauxia species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative hypoxylon canker (Biscogniauxia atropunctata), this species has more prominent bordered edges on its fruiting bodies and may appear slightly less uniform in texture.
